adoption.body: Businesses in the Census Bureau's survey report current AI use at 21.8%. Expected use within six months is 25.9%, but the measure records stated intent rather than current use. Near-term expectations therefore remain close to the current-use base.
adoption.headline: Business AI intentions sit just above reported current use

compute.body: Announced U.S. compute-manufacturing projects cover all four tracked critical AI supply-chain layers. The announced pipeline carries $362.0B of expected investment across 17 sites. Because these projects are announcements, the record does not establish installed or operating compute capacity.
compute.headline: Announced domestic projects span every tracked AI supply-chain layer

data_center.body: Available project records list 1,556 development sites, equal to 0.51x the operating-site count. The 287.2 GW published for development sites describes disclosed project scale, not energized load. Most active campus records lack a standardized published capacity figure, so aggregate pipeline scale remains only partly observable.
data_center.headline: Operating load remains unresolved in the development pipeline

finance.body: Across the sampled companies, operating cash flow equals 1.43x current capital spending. Cash reserves equal 0.96 years of current capital spending, a cushion against timing gaps. Forward commitments equal 5.04x current capital spending, far beyond the present reserve cushion.
finance.headline: Forward commitments extend funding needs beyond current capital spending

grid_storage.body: Active queue capacity records developer requests rather than operating supply. Most queued capacity remains outside executed-agreement or construction stages. Among projects in the 2000–2020 queue cohort, 13% reached operation. Queue size therefore speaks most directly to developer interest.
grid_storage.headline: Most queued capacity remains outside advanced stages

macro.body: Among companies sampled for AI-related financing, operating cash flow exceeds current capital spending. Cash reserves equal 0.96 years of that spending, whereas forward commitments equal 5.04 times it. The longer funding horizon reaches a physical boundary because data-center campuses with large electricity loads need delivered power, not generation plans alone. Power records list 227.0 gigawatts of net planned generation additions through 2030, not supply already placed in service. Published capacity for data-center campuses with large electricity loads describes project scale rather than energized load, leaving usable campus power unresolved. Delivered campus power can enable AI service without establishing how broadly businesses use AI. The Census Bureau’s business survey finds current AI use at 21.8% of businesses, and stated near-term intentions remain close to that base. Nonfarm-business productivity and real output both grew, although those measures do not identify AI as the cause. Reported business use cannot be treated as an economy-wide productivity result, even when AI provider revenue confirms paid demand. Current records locate the bottleneck at conversion evidence: they do not connect reported business use to an identifiable share of real output growth.
macro.headline: Funding commitments precede measurable economy-wide AI conversion

market.body: Among companies in the market sample, 69.6% posted positive returns over the year. Positive median and equal-weight returns over the same period further support breadth beyond a few market leaders. The ten largest companies account for 63.4% of sampled market value, so broad participation still sits within a concentrated valuation base.
market.headline: Equity gains extend beyond the largest sampled companies

power.body: Large-load campus records report 189,880 MW of published capacity, a project-scale disclosure rather than energized load. The generation pipeline contains 227.0 GW of net planned additions through 2030. Placement in service and delivery to the recorded campuses remain unresolved within the planned pipeline.
power.headline: Planned generation cannot establish delivered power for campuses

water.body: Direct facility-level water evidence covers 1.6% of 2,229 mapped data centers. The mapped records contain no quantified withdrawal or consumption values, so they cannot support a national facility-use estimate. Campus water availability remains unresolved by state-level drought exposure.
water.headline: Sparse disclosure obscures data-center water demand

workforce.body: Across 923 occupations in a static task benchmark, median software-adjusted large-language-model exposure is 45.8%. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel records positive employment growth. Computing infrastructure is the weakest tracked channel, whereas power and communication construction is the strongest. The benchmark measures work AI could affect without measuring automation or job loss.
workforce.headline: Tracked AI-linked labor channels show divergent employment direction

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The AI Equity Index fell materially to 32.7, while the average sector trading-pressure reading declined to 50.9. Positive one-year returns still extend to 62.7% of covered companies, and the median return is 14.3%, but both measures also declined materially. Recent reports framed the weakness around fears of slower AI spending. That reporting describes investor concern rather than a measured decline in spending.

headline.text: Market breadth weakens, although most covered companies remain positive over the year

body.text: Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, with capacity utilization at 81.7%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%, but utilization was lower at 72.2%. Output is rising in both industries, while the utilization gap indicates different pressure on installed capacity.

headline.text: Compute output is growing under different capacity conditions

body.text: Available project records list 3,068 operating sites and 1,556 in development, or roughly one development site for every two operating sites. Only 41.3% of active campus records include published capacity. The records therefore describe the breadth of the pipeline more clearly than its aggregate capacity.

headline.text: Capacity disclosure still covers less than half of active data-center campuses

body.text: Commercial electricity demand grew 3.0%, compared with 1.3% for total retail demand. Net planned generation additions edged up to 228.7 GW, but they remain a pipeline measure rather than delivered supply. Retail electricity prices rose 4.4%; that pace slowed materially, but prices are still increasing.

headline.text: Commercial power demand outpaces overall demand as price growth slows

body.text: Electric-power construction grew 8.0%, a material acceleration, while the active interconnection queue stands at 2,061 GW. Operating storage remains tilted toward shorter durations: its capacity-weighted average is 2.7 hours, and 45.5% of capacity can operate for at least four hours. MISO stakeholders reportedly called for better cost allocation for transmission spurred by large loads, placing the question of who pays alongside the physical expansion.

headline.text: Grid construction accelerates, but operating storage skews toward shorter durations

body.text: Current county drought data cover 1,434 of 1,482 data-center campuses, or 96.8%. The screen identifies 275 campuses in counties where some area is under D2-or-worse drought. This improves geographic exposure context, but county-level screening neither places each campus within the affected area nor measures facility water demand.

headline.text: County drought screening now covers nearly all mapped campuses

body.text: Among tracked AI-linked labor channels, only one has positive employment growth. That channel is power and communication construction, the strongest reading at 0.8%. Two channels have positive real-earnings growth. Employment gains are therefore confined to physical infrastructure, while earnings breadth also remains limited.

headline.text: The strongest tracked employment channel is growing just 0.8%
Physical indicators expand as AI equities cool and adoption edges higher

paragraphs.text: Investor confidence has cooled. The AI Equity Index and average sector trading-pressure reading both declined materially, while the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns fell to 62.7%. Recent reports framed the pullback around fears of slower AI spending, but those reports capture market concern rather than a measured contraction in investment. Operating cash flow still covers current capital spending by 1.42x, although lender strain increased materially.

Physical indicators still point to expansion. Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%, and electric-power construction grew 8.0%. Available data-center records list roughly one development site for every two operating sites, but only 41.3% of active campus records publish capacity. The generation pipeline contains 228.7 GW of net planned additions, leaving the record clearer about planned activity than about capacity ultimately delivered.

Deployment is advancing more gradually. Businesses report current AI use at 23.2%, while 27.3% expect use within six months, a gap of 4.1 percentage points. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth; even the strongest, power and communication construction, is growing 0.8%, and two channels show positive real-earnings growth. These measures do not yet show broad diffusion across businesses or the tracked labor channels.
